articles.headline: McIlroy four off lead on delayed first day in India
keyFacts: Rory McIlroy shot a two-under-par opening round of 70 to sit four shots behind clubhouse leader Niklas Norgaard at the DP World India Championship.
Thunder and lightning caused a four-hour suspension of play during the first round in New Delhi.
The first round will continue on Friday after being halted by weather delays.
body: DP World India Championship: Rory McIlroy four off clubhouse lead after thunder and lightning delays in first round

Weather caused four-hour suspension to play on Thursday in New Delhi; Rory McIlroy and Tommy Fleetwood finish on two under, four behind clubhouse leader Niklas Norgaard; first round continues on Friday; watch tournament until Sunday on Sky Sports Golf
Thursday 15 October 2026 14:10, UK
Rory McIlroy shot a two-under par opening round to finish four shots behind the clubhouse lead on a part-suspended first day of play at the DP World India Championship in New Delhi.
McIlroy was midway through the back nine when play was stopped for thunder and lightning in the area, with players then off the course for four hours.
When play did resume at 4pm local time, McIlroy completed a round of 70 to sit tied 13th.
The world No 2 started from the par-four 10th, which he bogeyed, and went out in 34 after birdies at the 13th, 15th and 18th.
He found another birdie at the second hole but followed that with a second bogey of the round at the third, before finishing with six successive pars.

Denmark's Niklas Norgaard holds the clubhouse lead on six-under thanks to a 66, with McIlroy's fellow Northern Irishman Tom McKibbin one of three players at five-under with Eugenio Chacarra, who is second in the Race to Dubai standings.
"Yeah, it was okay," McIlroy, who sits third in the Race to Dubai rankings, said of his first round.

"I felt like I hit the ball pretty well for the most part. Missed a few putts early on, got it going a little bit around the middle and then maybe missed a couple opportunities when we came back out after the delay.
"So overall, it felt like it could have been a couple better but still a solid start. No one's really getting away.

"The golf course is playing a little bit tougher than it did last year just with how long the rough is. So we'll see how much we play tomorrow, we're not sure. But yeah, it's a solid start and obviously still a lot of golf left to play."
Scottish trio Scott Jamieson, Ewen Ferguson and Bob MacIntyre all shot opening rounds of 68.
Tommy Fleetwood dropped two shots at his final hole, the ninth, to finish on two-under alongside McIlroy after finding the bushes with his tee shot and having to play out sideways.
Race to Dubai leader Patrick Reed was among the later groups to start after the weather delay and so only completed four holes, although was two-over already.
The final four groups did not tee off at all with the first round to resume on Friday.

articles.headline: Grand Theft Auto 6 launch trailer suddenly drops, showing a saucy shower scene, a tense police chase, and high-flying heists
keyFacts: Rockstar Games released the launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 ahead of its 19th November release on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.
The trailer showcases heists, a helicopter getaway, a shower scene between the two protagonists, and new music by Justice.
The trailer release coincides with an ongoing Rockstar employment tribunal in Glasgow and recent leaked gameplay videos.
body: Rockstar Games has released the launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 ahead of its 19th November release.

The trailer showcases the thrills set to come to the game on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S next month, with the footage itself apparently captured on the PlayStation 5. It features a selection of tidbits Grand Theft Auto fans may be interested in, including clips of heists in-action, one of which appearing to include a helicopter getaway gone awry.

There's also an intimate shower scene between the game's two protagonists, seemingly confirming the rumoured sex scenes and likely full nudity. There's a quick cut between a collection of other characters we'll run into, and various setpieces. Eagle-eyed viewers may spot some interesting details, including what appears to be an ankle tag on Lucia's leg, hinting she perhaps is out on parole. Jason also seems to get a reverse-charged phone call early on in the trailer, suggesting perhaps Lucia calling from jail.

The trailer opens with a shot of The Keys, a much-discussed portion of the GTA 6 that has been largely unexplored in prior trailers and gameplay footage. Also, the song playing in the background is a new standalone single from Justice called "Flower in a Hurricane", featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and the fantastic King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard.
The timing of the trailer is questionable, with Rockstar's employment tribunal ongoing in Glasgow, Scotland this week, and after a week of new leaked gameplay videos from the hacker Cyberleek.
As what is likely the final trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 before it releases, it's certainly a good tone setter for those eager to hop in.

articles.headline: Week 7 college football viewer's guide: With two top-10 matchups and four other top-25 games, get ready for an epic Saturday
keyFacts: Week 7 of the 2026 college football season features two games between top-10 teams and six matchups between AP Top 25 teams.
No. 5 Ohio State plays No. 6 Indiana in what marks the biggest home game in Indiana program history.
No. 2 Notre Dame plays No. 8 BYU in a top-10 matchup where Notre Dame is favored due to BYU missing player LJ Martin.
body: Welcome to the biggest weekend of the 2026 college football season. So far, anyway.
Week 7 features two games between top-10 teams and six games between teams ranked in the AP Top 25. With just five games featured, we had to cut one. And it was an incredibly tough decision.
If the football lives up to the hype on Saturday, it's going to be a great day. Here are our games to watch.
No. 5 Ohio State at No. 6 Indiana
If the Hoosiers win their 23rd straight game on Saturday, should they become the new No. 1 team in the country?

A big Georgia win probably keeps the Bulldogs in the top spot in Sunday's AP poll, but it's a conversation worth having. Ohio State would be a top-five win for an Indiana team that handed Nebraska its first loss of the season in Week 6 and also has a win over a ranked Northwestern team.

It's the biggest home game in Indiana history, too. The Hoosiers' previous massive regular-season contests have been on the road, in both Columbus in 2024 and Eugene in 2025 against Oregon. And they of course beat Ohio State 13-10 in Indianapolis in December in the Big Ten title game.

Given the way the Big Ten is unfolding this season, it's very likely that we're going to see these two teams back in Indianapolis in December. It's hard to pick anyone else at the moment.
Indiana's Josh Hoover hasn't thrown an interception while he has 17 TD passes on just 129 attempts. Ohio State QB Julian Sayin has also thrown 17 TDs, but he's done it on 34 more passes.

Ohio State's pass defense presents the biggest challenge of Hoover's career. Opposing QBs are completing just 53% of their passes for 151 yards this season. Illinois' Katin Houser is the only QB to throw for more than 200 yards this season against the Buckeyes, and a lot of those came late in a 23-point loss.

Can Ohio State run on Indiana? The Hoosiers are once again stifling opponents on the ground while the OSU tandem of Bo and Ja'Kobi Jackson — no relation — have rushed 138 times for 814 yards and 10 touchdowns so far this season for the Buckeyes. In the Big Ten championship game, Bo Jackson had 17 carries for 83 yards, but Indiana sacked Sayin five times. His ability to navigate the Indiana pass rush could be the Buckeyes' key.
No. 16 Mississippi State at No. 22 LSU

Will Kamario Taylor play on Saturday? The Mississippi State quarterback was listed as questionable as the Bulldogs come off their bye week. Taylor has been dealing with a foot injury and his status for the game truly does seem in question. The same goes for RB Fluff Bothwell, who left the Bulldogs' Week 5 loss to Alabama after getting one carry.
If they're out, the Bulldogs are in trouble. If they play, the chances of an upset are very real while LSU's hopes of immediate national contention under Lane Kiffin would further spiral.

It's fair to call Saturday's game a must-win for the Tigers. LSU has a schedule tough enough to get to the College Football Playoff with a 9-3 record. But at 4-2, LSU can only afford one more loss. And with games remaining against Alabama, Texas and Tennessee in November, is this Tigers team really going 3-0 in that stretch?

The LSU offense is averaging 6.5 yards a play, but has turned the ball over nearly twice a game thanks to Sam Leavitt's six interceptions. The former Arizona State quarterback has arguably been a more effective rusher than passer; he leads the team with seven rushing touchdowns and his 60 carries are second on the team behind Dilin Jones.

If there's a unit he can pick apart, it's the Mississippi State defense. The Bulldogs are allowing opponents to complete 63% of their passes and LaNorris Sellers, Austin Simmons and Keelon Russell each averaged over 7 yards an attempt.
No. 6 Alabama at No. 14 Tennessee
Welcome to the rivalry, George MacIntyre.

The sophomore QB made the first start of his career against Arkansas in Week 6 and was 18-of-20 passing for 247 yards with a TD and two interceptions. He replaced Faizon Brandon, who is listed as questionable on UT's availability report.

Alabama has at least one interception in each of its six games this season and has picked off just over 5% of opposing QB's passes. Though Georgia QB Gunner Stockton threw a pick in the Bulldogs' Week 6 win, he was incredibly efficient. Stockton finished with just four incompletions on 22 attempts as he threw for 249 yards and a TD.

It was also the second time this season that an Alabama opponent had rushed for 200 yards a game. The Tide have been stingy against the rush in its other four games — no one other than South Carolina and Georgia has averaged more than 3 yards a carry — but this could be a game for DeSean Bishop to carry the Tennessee offense if the Vols can pull the upset.
Bishop has rushed for 678 yards on just 107 carries and followed up his 220-yard performance against Auburn with 19 carries for 138 yards and a TD against Arkansas.

Alabama will be without star wide receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams after he suffered a lower-body injury against Georgia and was not 100% in the second half. Lotzeir Brooks has become the 1B to Coleman-Williams' 1A in the pass game, and Coleman-Williams' absence should open up more opportunities for WR Rico Scott and TEs Kaleb Edwards and Marshall Pritchett.
No. 13 Missouri at No. 9 Ole Miss

If you're wondering why the two best SEC games of the weekend are being played at the same time, it's because of the conference's scheduling philosophy. Earlier this year, the conference and ESPN designated gametime windows for every week of the season. Both Auburn's visit to Georgia and Mizzou's trip to Ole Miss were set as afternoon games, while the Alabama-Tennessee game was given a flex designation.

With Notre Dame playing at BYU — we'll get to that game in a moment — and ESPN having partial Big 12 rights, it was clear that the top-10 matchup in Provo would get the prime-time treatment. ESPN doesn't get the chance to have Notre Dame on its networks all that often.
Got that? OK, let's get to the game.

Three of the biggest offensive stars on the field will be playing against their former teams. Ole Miss RB Kewan Lacy began his career with the Tigers, while Missouri QB Austin Simmons and Tigers WR Cayden Lee both came to Mizzou from Ole Miss in the offseason.

The connection between Simmons and Lee has powered the Missouri pass game. Lee has 42 catches for 616 yards and has five touchdowns. He had seven career TDs over his first three seasons with the Rebels.

Lacy returned from a shoulder injury against Vanderbilt in Week 6 but he wasn't needed much in the blowout win. As the Rebels won 52-17, Lacy had seven carries for 39 yards and a TD. You might not find a better matchup between QB-RB duos all season in Ole Miss' Lacy and Trinidad Chambliss and Missouri's Simmons and Jamal Roberts, who is second in the country in rushing yards.
No. 2 Notre Dame at No. 8 BYU
This game would have a lot more luster if LJ Martin was available for the Cougars.

Yes, it's still a top-10 matchup, but there's a reason that Notre Dame is a double-digit favorite. Martin, the 2025 Big 12 offensive player of the year, is out after suffering a lower-body injury in the Cougars' win over TCU in Week 5.

Without Martin on the field, sophomore QB Bear Bachmeier was the entire offense against Iowa State last week. Bachmeier was 22-of-30 for 329 yards and two scores while also rushing nine times for 109 yards. Every other Cougar player combined for 20 carries for 74 yards. Bachmeier is going to have to get a lot of help against a Notre Dame defense that's one of the best in the country.

The Irish are allowing less than 60 rushing yards per game and just 4.1 yards a play. Yes, you can quibble with the quality of opponents Notre Dame has faced so far, but no one has gained more than 286 yards against the Irish in a game all season. That's incredibly impressive.

RB Aneyas Williams entered the season as the presumptive No. 1 back after the departures of first-round picks Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price. Instead, Williams has been the least-effective rusher on a per-carry basis among the Irish's top three backs.

Williams has 67 carries for 294 yards, while Nolan James Jr. has 65 carries for 335 yards. Jonaz Walton, meanwhile, has emerged as the team's leading rusher. After rushing 23 times for 120 yards against North Carolina, the freshman had 13 carries for 181 yards and two scores against Stanford. Will he get the start on Saturday night?
Other games to watch

Florida at No. 7 Texas (-10.5) (Noon ET, ABC): Both teams enter this game off embarrassing losses. Florida was smacked at home by a South Carolina team that was 0-3 in the SEC entering Week 6 and Texas' miscues gave Oklahoma all the opportunity it needed in a 27-24 Red River win. Given the way the Gators have looked over the last two weeks, this game feels like a Texas win. But we want to see more from the Texas offense.

North Carolina at Duke (-3.5) (3:30 p.m. ET, ESPN2): Are we setting up for another logjam in the middle of the ACC? Miami is clearly the best team in the conference, with Wake Forest emerging as the No. 2 team at the moment. But the Hurricanes are the only undefeated team in conference play through six weeks and 10 of the league's 17 teams have one conference loss. Duke and North Carolina are among that 10.

Florida State at No. 3 Miami (-21.5) (7 p.m. ET, ESPN): Yes, this spread is exceptionally large. But don't you want to see what Darian Mensah and Malachi Toney can do in a game that used to be one of the biggest of the season in the 1990s and early 2000s? A big Miami win will only raise more questions about the future of Florida State coach Mike Norvell , whose continued tenure may be more about university finances than anything else.

No. 15 Kentucky at Oklahoma (-7) (7:30 p.m. ET, SEC Network): What have the Sooners done to be giving the Wildcats a touchdown? The Oklahoma offense is still in rough shape. It got a special teams TD and a pick-6 in its win over Texas. A win for the Wildcats further establishes UK as a legit contender in the SEC — and backs up Will Stein's SEC media days confidence .

No. 18 Oklahoma State at No. 20 Houston (-4.5) (7:30 p.m. ET, Fox): This game just missed out on the cut for our top five. In any other week, it's a surefire inclusion. We've been bullish on the Cougars since the preseason and their blowout win over Kansas State solidified why. The winner of this game should deservedly be in the Big 12 title game conversation with Texas Tech, BYU and Utah. And don't be surprised if the victor actually appears in the game, too. If Martin is out for an extended period of time for BYU, it could be vulnerable. And Texas Tech doesn't look like the machine it was a season ago.

articles.headline: The next evolution of observability starts with telemetry
keyFacts: Technology environments struggle with fragmented telemetry, rising storage costs, and unclear signals due to collecting excessive and unfiltered data.
Organizations are shifting focus to process telemetry earlier in its lifecycle by filtering and enriching data before it reaches downstream systems.
Improved telemetry quality provides reliable information for AI-powered capabilities, leading to better operational trust and faster decision-making.
body: For technology teams, connecting telemetry has traditionally been seen as a route to greater visibility. The assumption is straightforward: the more information available about what is happening across an environment, the easier it should be to understand problems and respond to them.

But as modern technology environments have grown in scale and complexity, that equation no longer looks quite so simple and teams have found themselves dealing with fragmented telemetry and unclear signals. It now takes longer to understand what’s gone wrong, and even longer to fix it. And to add to the challenge further, the cost of storing and processing all this telemetry and data continues to be on the rise.
Vice President of Sales for Log Management at Dynatrace.

This is prompting organizations to reconsider where the problem should be addressed. Rather than collecting everything and attempting to make sense of it later, attention is shifting towards improving telemetry earlier in its lifecycle. Filtering, enriching and directing it from the outset can make the information reaching teams more relevant and ultimately easier to act on.
More data doesn’t always mean better insight

The volume of telemetry available isn’t the fundamental issue. Its quality is. As AI-driven capabilities become deeply embedded in software delivery and operations, the quality of observability telemetry becomes even more important. Collecting telemetry without filtering out what isn’t needed can leave employees spending more time managing information than extracting value from it.

Fragmentation makes this even more challenging. With data sitting across several tools and agents, each of which generates varied forms of signal and alert. When an outage occurs, teams may then need to piece together inconsistent information from across those tools before they can understand the root-cause of the problem. Consuming valuable time while the impact on the business continues to grow.

There is also a significant financial cost attached to this approach. Processing and storing telemetry and data at scale requires considerable resources, particularly when organizations are retaining information that contributes more noise than insight. In the traditional sense, this isn’t a technology problem. It’s a telemetry and data quality concern, and the longer it’s ignored, the worse it usually gets.
Rethinking where telemetry is processed

One way organizations are responding is by moving intelligence further upstream in the technology stack. In practice, that means making decisions about telemetry earlier – filtering out what isn’t useful, enriching important information and routing meaningful telemetry before it reaches downstream systems.

Teams are beginning to collect, process and route relevant observability telemetry in real-time before it is ingested into downstream systems. As a result, there is a less volume to handle, reduced expenses and cleaner telemetry to deal with since only the relevant signals are sent downstream.

Open standards such as OpenTelemtry are making it increasingly possible to take this approach across complex environments. They allow teams to gather telemetry consistently without being dependent on a particular vendor or set of tools. That flexibility is particularly valuable when working with intricate, distributed systems that span several clouds, security and storage platforms.
Furthermore, as environments continue to evolve, it makes adapting to them that much easier.
AI needs reliable information to make reliable decisions

The implications become particularly important as organizations introduce more AI-powered capabilities into their operations. AI systems depend on accurate, contextualized telemetry and data to produce insights and automate decisions.

Teams are not only slowed down by incomplete or cluttered telemetry, but it’s this simple: poor quality telemetry leads to poor quality insights. When those insights are applied to large-scale automated decision-making, the margin for error drastically lowers.

The same principle applies to trust. Teams responsible for automated systems need to understand what has happened and explain why decisions about performance or security have been made. Doing so becomes much more difficult when those decisions are based on inconsistent information.

And this requirement for confidence matters far beyond just the technical teams. As senior management and board members are being increasingly asked to support AI-driven decision making, they need to trust the information those decisions are built upon. Credible, consistent telemetry and data can make that conversation much simpler.

The operational advantages are also evident. Teams can work quicker if they aren’t continuously battling erratic telemetry and data. They spend less time on manual research, detect issues early, and automate with greater confidence.

A strong telemetry and data foundation and a unified, context-driven platform not only enhance daily operations but also increases the successes of the AI-powered capabilities the organization invests in over time.
Quality has to be built in from the beginning

Ultimately, faster innovation and better customer outcomes depend on organizations having useful telemetry and signals available when they are needed. The good news is that it doesn't require starting from scratch, it's about making choices early in the telemetry lifecycle.

By introducing intelligence at that stage, teams can improve the quality of what ultimately reaches their observability platforms and ensure it can scale as their environments grow. The advantage will not come from simply collecting more. It will come from ensuring the telemetry an organization does collect is relevant, trustworthy and ready to support action.

articles.headline: Jujutsu Zero Cursed Technique Tier List [🐺Shikigami]
keyFacts: Destructoid published a cursed technique tier list for the game Jujutsu Zero, ranking techniques from SSS-tier down to D-tier.
The article stated that Awakened V2 versions of cursed techniques, Ten Shadows, and Copy are among the best movesets in the game.
Players can farm Lumen for technique spins by exploring chests, using the AFK Realm, or completing raids.
body: The Awakened V2s of cursed techniques in Jujutsu Zero have brought a ton of power creep to the game. That said, some of the Awakened CTs really needed reworks and glow-ups. Keeping those in mind, here’s my Jujutsu Zero Cursed Technique tier list and guide .
Table of contents
Jujutsu Zero Technique Tier List
How to Farm Lumen in Jujutsu Zero
How to Farm Mastery in Jujutsu Zero
Jujutsu Zero Technique Tier List
All Jujutsu Zero Cursed Techniques Ranked
Roll on Banner/Special Grades can be exchanged at their NPCs/Some SGCT can come from Crates
⇓ The latest powercreep Meta movesets (All Awakened & Ten Shadows) ⇓
SSS Ten Shadows

One of the most versatile and powerful movesets thanks to Mahoraga A ton of move variety and utility with domain unlocked for different combos and unpredictability Is even stronger now with the October 10 Shikigami passive mechanic
Awakened Limitless

Awakening propels the old decent Limitless into a hard meta moveset The best AOE burst damage in the game with displacement and combo potential with the pull The Domain is OP with a full AOE stun and CD resets Combine with Six Eyes & Awakened Gojo Clan
Awakened Blood Manipulation

Incredibly flexible with Path 1 for sustained solo DPS, Path 2 for Siege and Raids and Path 3 for burst damage Combos with high-damage, stun, grouping and ranged options Great for Infinite and Overworld Raids/Bosses
Awakened Star Rage
The V2 brings Star Rage back from the dead You have a massive AOE damage cycle with all the moves that annihilates groups The move rotations and very easy to play and hit due to their range and AOE
Awakened Projection Sorcery

Best mobility and ton of different combo options with the Frame Freeze The stun moves allow you to accumulate damage while repositioning with base abilities for follow-ups The domain is also one of the best in the game with more stuns and a full CD reset to combo extend
⇓ The “old” Meta movesets that have been powercrept but are still really strong ⇓
S Copy

A very well rounded moveset with great melee but also ranged AOE moves Love Beam is excellent for PVE and Copy Cat can give you some nice utility from bosses for added mix ups The domain connects it all with stuns Even better with the recent Shikigami update
Shrine
Combine with the Sukuna Mark for a ton of AOE damage The best non-Awakened moveset for Raids and other game modes It’s weaker without the Sukuna Mark
Judgeman

A cycle of landing skills for the Guilty Bar for empowered moves which all deal great damage The Executioner sword is amazing for PVE since it deals %dmg to bosses and one shots NPCs A great PVE option overall but not the best for Investigations
Mythical Beast Amber
Amazing sustained DPS in mode, especially with Kashimo clan Excellent AOE moves for Raids Great for lower level players and scales well later on
⇓ Excellent Sub-Meta alternatives ⇓
A Solo Forbidden Area
An excellent utility and support option Gives you damage buffs and heals in the area Combos well with weapons Is more of a niche option and it sucks in Raids
Love Train
Can occasionally be one tier higher with good RNG since JAckpot boosts AOE damage of all moves That said it’s less reliable than other A-Tiers and all S-Tiers and above
Limitless
A decent overall AOE damage rotation that got powercrept You mainly want it for the Awakened version which is one of the best movesets in the game Otherwise, in base form, Shrine is much better
Cursed Energy Discharge
A viable mid-game PVE farming tool Okay damage and range There are better options with more combos in higher tiers since CED gets outscaled
⇓ Weaker than the above but still decently strong and just as fun to play ⇓
B Disaster Flames
A great beginner option for AOE damage and burns Gets outscaled fast in the late-game and raids
Projection Sorcery
Base Projection Sorcery is a decent moveset for Raids early on That said it gets outscaled easily if you don’t Awaken it
Disaster Tide
Similar case to Disaster Flame where it’s great for beginners starting out the game But you want to replace it with either S-Tier movesets or those that have Awakenings to be able to scale
⇓ Outdated movesets that either got awakenings or were left behind ⇓
C Blood Manipulation
Base Blood Manipulation is extremely underpowered That said it’s got one of the best Awakenings in the game
Star Rage
Star Rage is better than Ratio & Cursed Speech for early AOE farming It’s very easy to play and you want to go for its Awakening if you enjoy a simple AOE spamming playstyle
Ratio
Good AOEs for early game Replace when you can
Cursed Speech
The weakest of the usable CTs but still better than the two below
⇓ Drastically underpowered & practically unusable ⇓
D Straw Doll
The smallest amount of moves that hit unreliably
Explosive Flesh
Low DMG with big windups – unusable

In general, the best Cursed Techniques in Jujutsu Zero are the V2/Awakened versions of older CTs. Apart from those the best base form movesets are Ten Shadows and Copy with the October Shikigami passive updates. Shrine in combination with Sukuna’s Mark is also top-tier in Raids and pretty much all game modes.

articles.headline: Colorado urged to fire Deion Sanders and hire 13-win coach
keyFacts: Denver Post columnist Sean Keeler urged Colorado to fire football coach Deion Sanders and hire Jason Eck.
Sanders recently dismissed several players for behavior issues following a 41-7 loss to Northwestern.
Colorado is scheduled to host No. 11 Utah on Saturday night.
body: Deion Sanders always says the "standard is the standard." But what has that become for the Colorado Buffaloes? After posting five wins since the end of the 2024 season, the Buffaloes faithful are restless. Enough so, Denver Post columnist Sean Keeler has called for Sanders to be fired after three-plus seasons.

There was one name thrown out as a replacement, and he has ties to Colorado athletic director Fernando Lovo. "If the CU Buffs don’t make a run soon at Jason Eck, the poor man’s Curt Cignetti, some other Power 4 school looking to turn around its football program will snap him up," Keeler wrote.

"Sanders has three-and-a-half seasons left on a five-year, $54-million contract. If I’m Lovo, as my Buffs are getting ready to host No. 11 Utah late Saturday night, what have I seen from the past two years of The Coach Prime Era to convince me that Sanders is going to right this ship?"
Lovo hired Eck before leaving New Mexico in 2024. But would he do it again in Boulder? The former Idaho coach is 13-5 since taking over the Lobos from Bronco Mendenhall.
Winning Isn't the Only Thing in Boulder?

Sanders has never been afraid to demand more from his players. At Colorado, Coach Prime has built his message around discipline, accountability and representing something bigger than yourself. But when adversity strikes, the challenge becomes proving those principles can translate into a winning culture.

Following the disappointing loss to Northwestern in September, 41-7, Sanders confirmed that several players had been dismissed from the program because of a pattern of behavior he believed was cancerous to the team. He insisted the decision wasn’t simply about one defeat, but about preventing problems from growing into something bigger.
For Sanders, individual freedom cannot come at the expense of collective responsibility.
When Talent Isn’t Enough

Colorado’s struggles have made the distinction between individual ability and team discipline increasingly important. Recruiting talented players can raise expectations, but talent alone cannot guarantee execution, consistency or chemistry.

Sanders acknowledged that he had not intervened firmly enough when problems emerged during the previous season, when Colorado finished 3-9. Now, he wants to address the situation before it becomes even more escalated. The admission matters, leadership is not only about holding players accountable. It also requires a coach to recognize where his own decisions have fallen short.

Sanders has built his reputation on confidence and demanding standards. The next step is ensuring those standards are reflected in the team’s preparation, composure, and performance when the pressure rises.
The Culture behind the Spotlight

The attention surrounding Sanders often focuses on his personality, celebrity, and ability to turn Colorado into a national conversation. Yet the foundation of any successful program exists beyond the cameras. It’s built through daily habits, relationships and a shared understanding of what teammates owe one another.

Colorado’s defensive back Ben Finneseth publicly apologized for comments mocking the Wildcat’s temporary stadium. Sanders stood beside him as Finneseth acknowledged his mistake and promised to handle himself more maturely.

That moment offered another perspective on accountability. Correcting behavior doesn’t have to mean abandoning a player. It can mean demanding that the player acknowledge the mistake and learn from it. The challenge for Sanders is creating an environment where that accountability becomes part of the team’s identity, rather than something that only emerges after controversy.
Can Prime’s Principles Produce Progress?

Ultimately, Sanders will be judged by more than his speeches or disciplinary decisions. His culture must help Colorado become more competitive and consistent. This doesn’t mean every loss should reflect a broken locker room. However, it means the program must show progress in how it prepares, responds, and ultimately performs.

Sanders has made it clear that he won’t tolerate behavior that puts individuals' interests ahead of the team. Coach Prime has spent years teaching athletes to believe in themselves. Moving forward, his next challenge is getting an entire program to believe in the same standard. The culture isn’t about how loudly a coach demands accountability, it’s about whether the team lives by it when nobody is watching.
Colorado hosts No. 11 Utah on Saturday night (10:15 p.m. ET, ESPN).

articles.headline: TSMC sends scouts to check whether America's datacenters can deliver
keyFacts: TSMC is sending personnel to inspect United States datacenter construction and power availability as part of its plans for billions in new chipmaking capacity.
Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei stated during an earnings call that artificial intelligence demand continues to outstrip supply despite challenges in consumer markets.
TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of $46.72 billion, representing a 41.2 percent increase compared to the same period a year ago.
body: TSMC is dispatching personnel to check out US datacenter construction and power availability as it plans billions of dollars in additional chipmaking capacity. The Taiwanese chipmaking giant warned of pressure on consumer markets during its third-quarter earnings call, while maintaining that AI demand - at least for now - continues to outstrip supply. "Looking ahead, we continue to observe consumer and price-sensitive end market segments are being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties. As such, we are being prudent in our business planning going into 2027," said chairman and CEO C.C. Wei. Wei said AI demand remained strong, with CPUs for agentic workloads and networking chips adding to the need for silicon. "Therefore, semiconductors will remain essential in the AI mega trend. The value of semiconductors in the global supply chain is set to continue to increase in our view," he stated. TSMC expects capital expenditure of $60 billion to $64 billion this year. Spending across 2026-2028 is expected to exceed the total for 2023-2025 as it expands capacity for customers. Those plans depend on more than customers ordering chips: the datacenters housing them also need power, networking, memory, and other infrastructure. TSMC is checking how those pieces are coming together before committing to expanding capacity further. TSMC is planning roughly 20 leading-edge manufacturing and advanced-packaging facilities in Taiwan and overseas over the next several years, and Wei said the contract manufacturer is also focusing on capacity optimization across production nodes to generate more wafer output. One analyst on the earnings call asked whether power shortages, datacenter construction delays, advanced-packaging constraints, or limited supplies of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) could hold back projected growth. Wei said TSMC factors these constraints into its capacity planning. "We put every possibility we can, talking about the cloud service providers, capex, datacenter build-out, financial, power supply, and also other component supply, all into our consideration. "We make our own judgment, and then based on our assessment of the demand, we still think the demand is higher than the supply, and we are working very hard to narrow the gap." However, he declined to directly answer a question about whether he expected tightness in the wafer supply to be greater next year than this year, saying "the demand is extremely robust and getting higher and higher." Wei said preparations for A14, TSMC's next-generation process marketed as 1.4 nm, were underway. He expects it to become a bigger business than the current 2 nm generation. Risk production – an initial manufacturing phase ahead of commercial ramp-up – is scheduled for 2027, followed by volume production in 2028. For the third quarter ended September 30, 2026, TSMC reported revenue of $46.72 billion, an increase of 41.2 percent on the same period a year ago. Looking to the fourth quarter, the company expects another jump in revenue, to between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. At the midpoint, that would represent roughly 58 percent year-on-year growth. ®

articles.headline: Epic said its game launcher was faster than Steam on the same day Steam got a speed boost—so I've put both to the test
keyFacts: Epic stated on X that its game launcher is faster than Steam, coinciding with Valve releasing a Steam client update that improved startup performance.
A test conducted by PC Gamer found that the Steam client averaged 9.32 seconds to load, while the Epic Games Launcher averaged 5.98 seconds.
The author noted that closing the Epic Games Launcher is less straightforward than Steam because it continues running in the background unless task-ended.
body: Catching a glimpse of my screen is often a stressful experience for my colleagues. Besides my mess of desktop icons and all the browser tabs I have open at any given time, you don't want to know how many things I have set to launch on startup. Among these are, of course, the Steam and Epic Games Store clients and let me tell ya, not all launchers are created equal.

Earlier this week, Epic shared on X that it had "vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy." On the same day, Valve released a Steam Client update that "Improved Steam Client startup performance." Well, there's only one thing for it: I've got to benchmark these bad boys to determine once and for all whose launcher is actually faster.

For my basic benchmarks, I timed how quickly each client loaded into their respective storefronts (with all images displaying properly) after I opened them from the system tray (for those curious, my rig is this iBuyPower prebuilt with an RTX 4070 Super). I ran three tests on each and then took the average result. The Steam client loaded in 9.32 seconds on average, while the Epic Games Launcher loaded in 5.98 seconds for me.
Others have demonstrated Steam launching into the library in less time, but the Epic launcher is faster by seconds as far as my rig is concerned. That said, Steam remains my client of choice.

For instance, the first thing I noticed during my tests was that one does not simply 'exit' the Epic Games Launcher like you can with Steam. In Valve's client, you click 'Steam' in the top-left corner, then simply select 'exit' from the drop-down menu. A quick check of Task Manager shows it's not secretly running in the background.

It's not as straightforward for Epic. You can either click the 'x' or right-click the icon in your system tray and then select 'Close window'. But for my benchmarks, I opted to 'end task' the Epic launcher each time, as just closing the window doesn't stop it from running in the background. On each of my tests, I had to do this twice as the launcher opened itself after I ended the task the first time.

This small, very specific gripe aside, there are other features on Steam I personally appreciate. The recent Big Art update has really spruced up my game library, and I've been making liberal use of the 'personal calendar' feature (Steam has already spotlighted a number of upcoming cosy and horror games, much to my wallet's chagrin).
The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

As we've seen from my benchmarks, the Steam client is by no means perfect. For instance, Valve keeps saying it has fixed local game transfer quirks, though the experience can still be plenty quirky. I'm also not really a fan of the bouncing logo screensaver, either. And to be fair, even the features I like arguably make the client's store page look a bit cluttered. Still, I generally prefer that mess to the Epic Games Launcher's austere look myself.

Jess has been writing about games for over ten years, spending a significant chunk of that time working on print publications PLAY and Official PlayStation Magazine. When she’s not investigating all things hardware here, she's either constructing a passionate defence of a 7/10 game, daydreaming about her debut novel, or feeling wistful about the last time she chased some nerds around a field with an oversized foam sword.
