articles.headline: NVIDIA's RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI
keyFacts: Microsoft and NVIDIA introduced RTX Spark, a new system-on-a-chip combining Arm CPU cores, Blackwell GPU technology, and unified memory for Windows PCs.
NVIDIA claims RTX Spark systems deliver high efficiency for local AI tasks, content creation, and gaming while matching the performance of certain dedicated GPU laptops.
RTX Spark systems will launch this fall starting at $2,600, targeting developers and researchers who need large amounts of local memory.
body: NVIDIA's RTX Spark is good for Windows, even if you don't need local AI
Windows PCs may finally catch up to Apple Silicon.

Last week, I spent two days hearing how Microsoft and NVIDIA are "reinventing the PC" with RTX Spark, the new system-on-a-chip powering the Surface Laptop Ultra and several other Windows PCs this fall. It's the first time we've seen powerful Arm CPUs joined together with NVIDIA's Blackwell GPU technology and up to 128GB of ultra-fast unified memory on a single chip. Theoretically, RTX Spark should allow for thin-yet-powerful laptops (and a few small desktops) that can handle AI tasks locally, as well as tackling content creation and gaming. So sure, I suppose NVIDIA and Microsoft have a reason to gloat a bit.

But, just like the launch of Snapdragon-powered Copilot+ systems two years ago, it was hard to ignore the elephant in the room: RTX Spark is clearly a response to Apple Silicon and the transformational changes it brought to Macs six years ago. Apple's chips are also made up of a powerful Arm CPU, capable GPU and fast unified memory, and they span the company's lineup from the tiny Mac mini to the super-powerful Mac Studio and 16-inch MacBook Pro. With RTX Spark, Windows users finally have a way to see the benefits of an efficient Arm-based SoC on high-end PCs, while the recent batch of Qualcomm chips covers the low-end and mid-range.

There weren't many surprises at Microsoft's AI launch event (featuring the Surface Laptop Ultra), or at NVIDIA's RTX Spark Editor's Day, which I attended alongside other media and analysts. Both companies want to sell us a future where we can run AI models and agents right from an RTX Spark-powered Windows laptop, something that seemed clear since the chip was announced at Computex. But even if that future doesn't come to pass, RTX Spark could still lead to some intriguing changes in the PC world.
Under the hood with RTX Spark

The RTX Spark SoC is powered by up to 20 NVIDIA Grace Arm CPU cores (10 performance cores and 10 efficiency cores), a Blackwell GPU with up to 6,144 CUDA cores, and up to 128GB of unified LPDDR5x memory running at 9,400 Mbps. There's also a slightly less powerful configuration with 18 CPU cores and 5,120 GPU cores. RTX Spark also includes much of what you'd find on NVIDIA's latest GPUs, including fifth-gen tensor cores, fourth-gen ray tracing cores, and a Blackwell video engine (with support of AV1 UHQ and 4:2:2 encoding and decoding).

By shoving all of this hardware onto a single chip, NVIDIA claims the RTX Spark is twice as efficient as a laptop powered by an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H and RTX 5070 dedicated GPU, while gaming at 60 watts. NVIDIA has previously said RTX Spark systems should be similarly powerful to RTX 5070 laptops, though as you can tell from the chart below, those dedicated GPU systems can also draw a lot more energy for better performance.

If you plan to be connected to power most of the time and don't need to travel with your laptop, you may see little benefit from choosing an RTX Spark system. But if you need to do serious creative work on the go, RTX Spark's improved efficiency allows PCs to work as fast on battery as they are while plugged in, according to NVIDIA. From my brief time with the Surface Laptop Ultra, I didn't notice any performance drops while playing Gears of War: E-Day on battery power. The game still looked silky smooth in 1440p with high graphics settings.
RTX Spark is built for AI, but also helps content creation and gaming

With its support for tons of unified RAM, RTX Spark systems should appeal to AI developers and researchers who need as much memory as they can to run large AI models locally, like the 125B parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. An RTX Spark system could significantly reduce the amount of money spent on cloud AI tokens, or replace that demand entirely. One researcher I spoke with was jealous that his colleagues were able to easily run AI models on modern Mac laptops, and he was excited about the possibility of doing the same on a Windows notebook. RTX Spark is also coming along as Microsoft is adding more support in Windows 11 for on-device AI tools like Perplexity, as well as simplified ways to set up AI agents like OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot.

Not surprisingly, NVIDIA is also touting RTX Spark's gaming capabilities. Since it features a Blackwell GPU front and center, it'll deliver all of the features you'd expect from RTX 50-series cards, including support for DLSS 5. As I mentioned before, you can expect performance similar to an RTX 5070 — NVIDIA is specifically touting 1440p as the intended resolution for RTX Spark systems, though I'd be interested to see how they perform in 4K with DLSS. A new performance mode for DLSS Frame Generation can push Cyberpunk 2077 up to 280fps with 6x frame gen, compared 213fps without performance mode. (It's unclear what you lose to achieve that frame bump, though.)

Since RTX Spark is Arm-based, it won't natively run every game on Windows, but NVIDIA claims recent titles like Control Resonant and the aforementioned Gears of War: E-Day will be supported at launch thanks to Microsoft's Prism emulator for x86 software. NBA 2K27, the main DLSS 5 launch game, will also be supported, alongside World of Warcraft: Forever. NVIDIA says it's also working with major anti-cheat providers to support their products, something that's prevented multiplayer games from working on Arm Windows systems in the past.

I'll have to spend more time with RTX Spark systems to see how well they actually handle gaming, beyond my minutes with Gears of War: E-Day. But if playing games is a priority, you'd still be better off with an Intel or AMD system with a dedicated GPU. At least then you wouldn't have to worry about potential emulation issues.

RTX Spark systems will also be useful content creation — again, as you'd expect from PCs with RTX Blackwell GPUs. You can lean on hardware acceleration in tools like Blender, and notably, Adobe is re-architecting Photoshop and Premiere specifically for NVIDIA's platform. That's a major sign of faith from one of the biggest software companies around, though I suppose Adobe is also reading the tea leaves and seeing a bright future for Arm-based Windows systems in general.
RTX Spark isn't for everyone, but that's okay

NVIDIA isn't targeting casual consumers with RTX Spark, not with a starting price of $2,600 for 18-core systems, or an eye-bleeding $3,700 for the full-powered 20-core models. Both NVIDIA and Microsoft are targeting AI developers and researchers who have the money to spend on insane amounts of RAM. And they should be prepared to open their wallets — a Surface Laptop Ultra with 128GB of RAM will cost a smooth $5.900. Still, that's a good deal cheaper than a fully-equipped M5 Max 16-inch MacBook Pro with 128GB of RAM, which costs $7,000.

Simply by existing, the RTX Spark platform will likely push Intel and AMD in creative new directions. AMD is trying to accomplish something similar with its Ryzen AI Max 400 chips, which can also house a ton of unified memory, but can also run existing x86 software without any emulation. And Intel has been eager to prove itself against AMD for the last few years, which has resulted in its powerful Core Ultra Series 3 chips. As always, competition is great for consumers.

articles.headline: Xreal’s New High-End Display Glasses Get a Brightness Boost
keyFacts: Xreal released the $599 Xreal One Pro Plus display glasses, featuring an increased brightness of 1,200 nits.
The new glasses include improved visual modes, better room light blocking, and a smoother AI 3D conversion mode.
The author reported that the glasses remain tethered via USB-C and share a similar design to their predecessor.
body: The quality of plug-in display glasses has gotten seriously good lately, if you can put up with the idea of resting your monitor on your face. The price for good glasses has been dropping (down to $299 for some notable ones), but the pricier top-end models have advantages.

The new $599 Xreal One Pro Plus glasses, available now, offer a few subtle upgrades to last year’s model. I’ve been trying a pair out and the experience is largely the same, just a bit better (namely, brighter).
What’s new: Brightness, a few new visual modes

The previous Xreal One Pro display glasses were one of my favorite pairs around, along with the Viture Beast ones. In the past, Xreal’s design was thinner and lighter than Viture’s, but they had a notably dimmer display. That’s been fixed now with the One Pro Plus, which have 1,200 nits of brightness (versus 700 for the One Pro display glasses). There are also a few more visual settings, including “Reading,” which seems to move the virtual display a bit closer.
More from CNET

The One Pro Plus also have a smoother AI 3D conversion mode that turns any 2D image or video (or connected game) into 3D. The effect runs at a smoother frame rate than before, but the conversion still feels imperfect and gimmicky and compromises the frame rate too much compared with leaving it off.

But the rest of these glasses are similar to their predecessor. They still need to be tethered via USB-C cable to whatever laptop, phone or game console you have around, and they still project their displays down from the top of the glasses through half-mirror lenses that make the display feel overlaid in front of your eyes. They’re not any more portable or differently designed than before, and still resemble odd sunglasses. (They do pack up easily into an included case, though.) They have the same onboard chip that can pin displays in place when you turn your head, along with the same ability to change the size and perceived distance of the virtual display, including widescreen modes for connected computers.
The included nose pads are slightly more comfortable, and the arms can still bend at different angles for a proper fit.
Wearing the Xreal One Pro Plus

I’ve been wearing the One Pro Plus with prescription lens inserts while writing this story on a MacBook, and the differences are subtle. But I appreciate the extra brightness, and the electrochromic dimming seems to block out room light even better. Together, those improvements make the glasses much more effective in brightly lit rooms or outdoors.
I also watched some of the indie horror movie Buddy on my iPhone, and the more vivid display made the glasses feel like a more effective personal cinema.

I played Star Wars Galactic Racer on Steam Deck with these on my face, too, and had a blast. The display is crisp and vivid, although after swapping back and forth with the Viture Beast, I prefer the Beast slightly for its larger-feeling display.
The audio on the speaker arms sounds fine, but isn’t any better than the Xreal One Pro’s audio. When I wear them, I prefer to use AirPods for audio.

I liked the Viture Beast for their bright, micro-OLED display and their stepped-up screen resolution, which has an aspect ratio that works better for gaming (1,900×1,200). The 1,250 nits on the Beast are pretty close to Xreal One Pro Plus, though.

My issue is that Xreal has so many display glasses options now that it’s getting confusing, including a pair made with Asus, a more affordable pair released earlier this year and a mixed reality computer-glasses system called Xreal Aura that was made with Google, costs $1,279 and is arriving later this fall.

With the One Pro Plus, Xreal has made the best display glasses I’ve ever worn next to Viture Beast, and their smaller on-face feel is more comfortable. But if you’re looking to see what glasses tech has in store next, you might want to see what the Xreal Aura offer. I’ll be reviewing them soon.

articles.headline: Google’s new Universal Cart tracks prices on items you want now – plus 3 other tricks
keyFacts: Google introduced online shopping tools, including the Universal Cart and When to Buy Guide, using search data and artificial intelligence.
Google stated that the Universal Cart saves items across retailers, tracks prices and inventory, identifies savings, and integrates with Google Pay.
Google said the tools provide shoppers with convenience and confidence during the holiday shopping season.
body: October Prime Day kicked off the early holiday shopping season last week, and now Google is introducing new tools for online shoppers. Google’s latest tools use Google Search data and AI-powered item organization.

Google’s new When to Buy Guide and Universal Cart may help alleviate the stressful holiday dilemmas we see year after year by advising you when certain items are discounted and saving your items from different retailers in one place, respectively.
More from ZDNET
1. Save products from multiple retailers

Google’s Universal Cart lets you ditch open tabs and endless screenshots. The cart can save your progress across Google, so you’re never starting from scratch. Every time you save a product to your cart via AI Mode in Search or the Gemini app, it will be waiting for you when you return or decide to check out.
2. Keep tabs on pricing or inventory

Google’s cart is built on the 60+ billion continually refreshed product listings via Google’s Shopping Graph. This means that you can get notifications about price drops or restocks without doing any extra work — Universal Cart is continually checking for you in the background.
3. Identify hidden savings or points from your cart

Google’s cart doesn’t just house products you’re eyeing. It can help you buy smarter by maximizing the benefits you may already have. For example, the Universal Cart can help you identify the specific benefits of each payment option you may have, including card perks, and help you choose which one is best to use if you decide to purchase. Universal Cart is built on Google Wallet, making it more convenient for those using Google’s shopping tools and payment methods. Plus, the cart will also identify any relevant promo codes so you can save more.
4. Make seamless, trusted purchases

Universal Cart seamlessly integrates with Google Pay in just a few taps right within the cart, or shoppers can transfer their items directly to merchant carts to complete their purchase on the merchant’s site. Either way you choose, you’ll receive full communication about orders and customer support from the merchant you checked out with, which is the seller of record.
Google said that as the holiday season warms up, Universal Cart is one way to give “shoppers the convenience and smarts they need to make the best shopping choices.”

Google’s When to Buy Guide is a new report that analyzes historical promotional patterns, search trends, and discount data across US merchants. This year’s insights include when the best time is to snag signature scents, why you should reconsider buying that handbag on Black Friday, and why shopping early for travel gear like suitcases is better if you’re an early bird.

Google said in its press release that the company is building the future of commerce across two specific fronts: “Unlocking agentic capabilities that act on your behalf and designing practical tools that give shoppers confidence and control. Google’s Universal Cart is built for that second track — mirroring how people actually shop today across Google, without losing track of their items, their savings, or the merchants they trust.”

articles.headline: "I lost the concept of home, until my grandmother took me into these forests" - Trollheim: Gnomes is a survival game from ex-DICE and Paradox devs that channels childhood fairytales
keyFacts: Swedish studio Off-leash Interactive and publisher Fireshine Games announced the survival-crafting game Trollheim: Gnomes.
Developers from DICE and Paradox are creating the game, which is based on Nordic folklore and childhood memories.
The game features an eight-player multiplayer mode, base building, and exploration without a specific release date announced.
body: Swedish studio Off-leash Interactive and Denshattack publishers Fireshine Games have announced Trollheim: Gnomes, a survival-crafting fairytale in which you, a three-inch-high gnome, explore a procedurally generated forest derived from Nordic folklore. You'll be clambering up enormous trees, lighting campfires beneath mushrooms, and befriending or evading troublesome larger supernatural creatures known as "Väsen".

I caught a briefing for Trollheim: Gnomes earlier this month, and while I worry this is generic fare on some level, I'd sure like to get lost in those procgen woods. I'm also interested in the game's eight-player multiplayer, in that it seemingly creates opportunities for hide-and-seek – the game's building system affords scope to camouflage your dwellings against the litter, moss and mold of the forest floor.

Off-leash are a new studio founded by some fairly seasoned people. Trollheim game director Jojje Dalunde spent nine years at Battlefield creators DICE, while company CEO Jakob Munthe is a former executive producer at Paradox Interactive. Munthe's most recent credits include Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines 2, which I guess isn't necessarily reassuring, but hey, that game didn't turn out too terribly in the end. Art producer Josefin Lindgren has done stints at Payday household Starbreeze and Unravel developers Coldwood Interactive. I can definitely make out a thread between Unravel's homespun countryside and Trollheim's pungent array of organic terrain and building materials.

Trollheim: Gnomes is the first project in a narrative universe founded by film-maker Björne Larson. He and other members of the Gnomes team are piping their own childhood memories of Nordic woodland lore into the game. "When my parents divorced, I lost the concept of home, until my grandmother took me into these forests we grew up in, telling me about the gnomes and trolls and fairies who lived there and thrived there," Larson told journalists during the briefing. "Ultimately the forest made me feel at home, and cared for."

As you might expect from that personal reflection, Gnomes isn't a combat-led game, though it begins with scenes of strife: the Sprýg Gnomes are driven out from Midgård by a corrupted Oden, forced to relocate to the wildwoods of Trollheim. The non-player denizens of the woods can be threatening – hungry trolls may go after your food, for example - but the Väsen are broadly characterised as "neighbours", not enemies. Your job is to find your niche alongside them.

You might be able to placate grumpier Väsen with the help of other players. During the briefing, the developers gave the example of snaring a troll with rope trap, calming the beast with some flute music, and then offering them a tasty stew. The game's gifting system strives to make an art out of reviving downed players and NPCs: you'll need to identify and prepare an appropriate remedy, though Off-leash didn't go into detail here. As for player specialisation: there are no classes, so it's all about what you craft and wear.

The environment itself is pretty enchanting. I guess Obsidian's Grounded is the immediate comparison, but Grounded doesn't have trunks this overwhelmingly tall. A lot of work has gone into capturing both the scale of the canopy and the minutiae of twigs, berries, fungus and boulders. There are babbling brooks and moonlit lakes that are crying out for a birchleaf canoe (I'm not sure boating is a thing in the game). There are undulating mossy carpets that look like they'd wrench the ankles of any human hikers, but seem pleasant enough to scramble over when you're the size of a champagne cork.

Sadly, the inclusion of elements familiar from other open world and survival games tramples some of the charm. You can swoop with a hang-glider purloined from The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and there's the usual survival game building system of clipped-together holographic templates, which wrecks the illusion of assembling dwellings from bits of sylvan detritus. That's an impression based on hands-off play, mind. When I told the devs I found the building system a bit of a letdown, they argued that the small scale and level of creative control add up into something distinctive.

The gnome architectural designs look lovely in themselves, and again, I'm keen on the prospect of concealing them in amongst the roots of spruce and pine. Or constructing nests linked by ropeways, high up in the branches. I don't think there's PVP, as such, and I'm not sure the game's NPCs can be duped by camouflaged exteriors, but I like the idea of tribes of players hiding out from each other, or leaving intricate trails to their lairs. If you're an especially insular species of gnome - a proper Svirfneblin - you can play the whole thing solo and offline.
Read more about Trollheim: Gnome on Steam. There's no release date yet, but they're taking applications for a playtest. Meet you under the third toadstool on the left, eh? I'll bring my flute.

articles.headline: Starlink: How Elon Musk's company influences geopolitics
keyFacts: Elon Musk's Starlink provides satellite-based internet access in remote regions, disaster zones, and conflict areas globally.
The satellite system has been deployed in Ukraine, Iran, Sudan, Venezuela, and Gaza for military, humanitarian, or protest communications.
Critics and officials have raised concerns about SpaceX's geopolitical influence, environmental impacts, and potential ecological consequences.
body: Lack of internet access is a major problem in many regions of the world today.

Starlink was initially developed by the American tech billionaire Elon Musk to solve this problem. It was designed as a way of quickly getting the internet into regions all over the world where this was either impossible to do by conventional methods, or so expensive that it wasn't worth attempting.

Since then, Starlink's field of application has widened significantly. It's used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments.
But there is a downside: Ukraine's military, for example, is heavily dependent on Musk's satellite system. This has become especially apparent as the service faces external disruption.
How does Starlink work?

Starlink, which is operated by Musk's SpaceX company, is a satellite-based system consisting of 10,000 small satellites located around the world. They transfer data packages via laser links and do not require a constant, direct visual link to a ground station.

Unlike other internet satellites, which orbit at around 36,000 kilometers (22,000 miles) above the Earth, Starlink satellites are only about 550 kilometers up. This means they can transmit internet signals much faster than the others.

All users need is a small receiver terminal with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically steers toward the satellites as they pass overhead. The terminals receive signals from these satellites and transmit them to a nearby router, which supplies the broadband internet connection.
Where has Starlink already been deployed?

Ukraine: Since the start of the Russia's full-scale war in February 2022, Starlink has become a vital instrument of communication in the war zone. The Ukrainian armed forces use Starlink to coordinate units, operate drones and control unmanned ground systems. In the civilian sector, the system is used by hospitals, emergency services, energy suppliers and the railway network.
Ukraine offers a particularly vivid example of how heavily its military capabilities now depend on Starlink.

In mid-October, Ukrainian army units reported disruptions to data transmission, which are said to have severely affected the control of combat, interceptor- and reconnaissance drones. Elon Musk said that restrictions on the speed and use of Starlink are determined by the US military and ultimately the US president. At this stage, it remains unclear who ordered the restrictions.

Iran: In early January 2026, protests erupted all across the country against the regime in Tehran. The government's hardline response included a nationwide internet shutdown. Reportedly, thousands of Starlink terminals were smuggled into Iran and sold on the black market. This enabled the protest movement to go on coordinating demonstrations against the regime, using Starlink to circumvent state censorship of the internet.

The country's authorities are cracking down on the satellite service and its users. Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace, described Starlink as a hostile "tool of war" and said the regime had means at its disposal to disrupt satellite connections.

Starlink is officially banned in Iran. Anyone using the service faces a prison sentence of six months to two years. If users are also charged with endangering national security or espionage, the offence can even carry the death penalty.

Sudan: In the Sudanese civil war, Starlink is used primarily by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group fighting against the internationally-recognized government. Hundreds of devices were smuggled into the country via the United Arab Emirates, and there is now a thriving black market for Starlink terminals in Sudan. The RSF use them to communicate and coordinate with their militias, while the Sudanese Armed Forces are trying to block both the import and use of the terminals.

Venezuela: Here too, Starlink has been used in the past to sidestep information blackouts and secure access to the internet. For a long time, the service was only available unofficially, by buying kits from local dealers. Following the US intervention in early January 2026, during which then-head of state, Nicolas Maduro, was taken prisoner, Musk offered the people of Venezuela a month's free broadband internet service via Starlink.

Gaza: Starlink has been used for humanitarian purposes in the devastated Gaza Strip since July 2024. Aid organizations and a field hospital use it to facilitate telemedical assistance and logistical coordination. Access for civilians remains limited because of Israeli security concerns.
Why has Starlink been criticized?

Starlink is often the only way to access the internet in conflict zones. This gives Musk and his operating company SpaceX tremendous influence. Previously, for example, Musk refused to activate Starlink in Ukraine to enable an attack in Crimea. US President Donald Trump has also threatened to switch off the satellites in Ukraine, as a way of forcing Kyiv to make concessions in peace negotiations.

There has also been criticism from an ecological perspective. The Starlink satellites have a lifespan of less than five years. Every day, on average, one or two of them burn up in the Earth's atmosphere. This releases aluminum oxide, which could affect the ozone layer, contributing to global warming. In addition, all those thousands of satellites reflect the sunlight, making the night sky brighter, and this may also have repercussions for the world's animals.
Any Starlink alternatives?

In an effort to break Starlink's monopoly, other companies, especially in Europe, are already working on alternatives. At present, the biggest private competitor to SpaceX is a company called Eutelsat. With a fleet of over 600 satellites, its OneWeb service is far smaller, focusing on business customers and maritime use.

But Eutelsat is also involved in the development of IRIS2 — an acronym for Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite, an ambitious EU project to establish a highly secure satellite network. The aim is to make Europe less dependent on Starlink, but IRIS2 won't be fully operational before 2032.

Elon Musk also has competition inside the US from another billionaire, Jeff Bezos, whose company Amazon is currently working on Amazon Leo, known until recently as Project Kuiper. This is establishing a network of more than 3,200 new low-Earth-orbit satellites. Amazon plans to roll out the service later this year in the US, Canada, France, Britain and Germany.

The sky is clearly getting crowded. China is also refining two satellite communications systems of its own. Guowang, a state project conceived primarily for national and military purposes, will consist of up to 13,000 satellites, while another project, Qianfan, with an estimated 12,000 satellites, is more commercially oriented and aims to provide services to newly industrialized and developing countries. The first mass starts for both of these projects are planned for this year.
This article has been translated from German.
Editor's note: This piece was originally published on February 14, 2026. It was updated on October 15, 2026, to reflect recent developments.

articles.headline: Obama's billion-dollar baby: Chicago center's price tag hits monumental milestone, tripling original estimate
keyFacts: The Obama Presidential Center construction costs reached approximately $1 billion, nearly tripling original estimates, according to the Obama Foundation.
Some construction subcontractors said they are still fighting to recover millions of dollars in disputed payments for their work.
Obama Foundation officials said they plan to make significant investments into the center's endowment fund in coming years.
body: The price tag for the beleaguered Obama Presidential Center is now projected to top $1 billion, nearly triple its original estimate, the foundation overseeing construction of the Chicago facility told Fox News Digital.

Confirmation of the 10-figure cost marks another chapter in the troubled history of the much-delayed project, which opened five years behind schedule amid controversy over its use of public parkland and claims that subcontractors were stiffed out of millions of dollars. It comes as newly released financial records reviewed by Fox News Digital offer a fresh look at the finances of the Obama Foundation, the former president's private nonprofit that oversaw construction of the billion-dollar project.

The sprawling campus on the Windy City's south side was originally expected to open in 2021, with construction costs estimated at $300 million to $350 million. But years of federal reviews, legal challenges and construction delays preceded its eventual opening in June 2026, by which time projected costs had skyrocketed to approximately $850 million.

Hailed by Democrats and supporters as a historic investment in the community and a tribute to the former president's legacy, the center was promoted as a catalyst for jobs, economic growth and new opportunities for underserved communities.
BUREAUCRATS HIDE TRUE PRICE OF OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER AS TAXPAYERS HIT WITH INFRASTRUCTURE BILL

"While we continue to reconcile costs and plan ahead for additional capital improvements, we anticipate our total cost for constructing the campus is approximately $1 billion — again, all raised in private contributions," Emily Bittner, the Obama Foundation's vice president of communications, told Fox News Digital. "This includes investments in additional public art, insurance, scope changes in our Home Court, project management and exhibit installation, among other categories."

The campus serves as both a museum dedicated to Obama's presidency and the headquarters of the Obama Foundation. It also features a public library branch and an athletic center, but unlike traditional presidential libraries, it does not house his original presidential records, although digital versions and artifacts are featured in its museum.

The climb toward the $1 billion mark has seemed inevitable in recent years, with approximately $909 million in construction-related costs recorded by the end of 2025, when the project was about 80% complete, according to its newly released audited financial statements.

The Obama Foundation's newly released financial disclosures cover the nonprofit's entire operation, not just the Chicago campus. It also runs leadership, education and community programs across the United States and around the world.

The tax filings show donations and grants fell to approximately $151 million in 2025, down from $195 million in 2024. Fundraising has fluctuated sharply in recent years, falling from $311 million in 2022 to $129 million in 2023 before rebounding in 2024 and declining again last year.
OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER SUBCONTRACTORS FILE FRESH PAYMENT CLAIMS TOTALING NEARLY $900K
Total liabilities climbed to approximately $103.5 million in 2025, during the final stages of the center's construction, up from $35 million in 2024 and $20 million in 2022.

The Obama Foundation's outstanding borrowing also rose from $15 million at the end of 2025 to approximately $63.5 million by July 2026, according to its audited financial statements. The nonprofit said it borrowed the money to cover short-term costs during the final stages of construction and that the loans were not secured against its rights to the property.
Its money and investments available to cover everyday expenses also fell from approximately $265 million in 2024 to $101 million in 2025.

Brian Mittendorf, a nonprofit accounting professor at the Ohio State University who reviewed the Obama Foundation's tax filings and audited financial statements, said the nonprofit remains on solid financial footing, with more than $1.1 billion in net assets at the end of 2025.

"In terms of the organization's overall financial health, again, I would say financial health looks quite good," Mittendorf told Fox News Digital. "They have a decent amount of cash, investments, liquidity, and so on. So it's not like they're in financial difficulty by any means."
However, he noted that much of the foundation's wealth is tied up in the Presidential Center, rather than assets that could readily be converted into cash.

"Bottom line to me: I don’t see a short-term financial distress here, but I do see an organization that has tied up a lot of its resources in its buildings, which means more costs to come and the need for more revenues to make this sustainable," he said.
OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25
Mittendorf warned that raising money to maintain the sprawling campus could prove more challenging than funding its construction.
"It's much easier to raise money when it's for building a building than it is for doing upkeep or paying for insurance or paying utilities," he said.
Obama Foundation officials said its operating costs are covered by revenue and private donations, although they did not provide a figure for the center's annual operating and maintenance expenses.
The Obama Presidential Center sits on 19.3 acres of historic public parkland in Jackson Park. It secured the site through a 99-year agreement with the city for a one-time payment of just $10.
While the foundation funded construction, the land and buildings are legally owned by the City of Chicago.

Critics have long raised concerns over the foundation's failure to fully fund a proposed $470 million endowment — a financial safety net designed to generate income for the center's upkeep and reduce the risk of taxpayers footing the bill if the project runs into trouble.

A previous Fox News Digital investigation found that just $1 million had been set aside for years. Newly released financial statements show the Foundation's overall endowment grew to approximately $14.2 million by the end of 2025, although it remains unclear how much of that money is specifically reserved for the Presidential Center.

Obama Foundation officials said the agreement with the city of Chicago required them to establish an endowment, not fully fund it, before taking control of the site. They said they prioritized fundraising for construction and leadership programs and that they plan to make significant investments in the fund in the coming years.

Richard Epstein, a New York University law professor who has advised opponents of the project, disputed the Obama Foundation's interpretation, arguing that establishing an endowment without adequately funding it defeats its purpose.

"Otherwise, they provide no protection," Epstein told Fox News Digital, arguing that under the Obama Foundation's interpretation, "they could list the endowment as $1 billion and fund it with ten cents."

Despite the foundation's substantial assets, some of the subcontractors who helped build it say they are still fighting to recover millions of dollars in disputed payments. A previous Fox News Digital investigation identified several firms claiming major financial losses, including minority-owned businesses the project was intended to support.

Mike Owen, owner of Chicago-based Adamson Plumbing, said his company suffered nearly $4 million in losses tied to the project, forcing him to suspend operations and lay off 25 union workers . His company subsequently filed a $1.72 million mechanics lien seeking payment for disputed work.
Owen told Fox News Digital this week that he still has not recovered the money he is seeking.

The Obama Foundation previously said Lakeside Alliance, the project's construction manager, was responsible for managing and paying subcontractors and that the foundation had no outstanding disputed charges with the alliance. Lakeside Alliance has said contractual closeout on a project of this scale can continue long after opening and that it remains committed to resolving outstanding matters.

The campus features a museum dedicated to Obama's presidency, housed in a 225-foot-tall, eight-story tower, along with a branch of the Chicago Public Library, a children's playground, an auditorium, conference and meeting spaces, public gardens and more than 20 commissioned art installations.

At the southern end of the campus sits Home Court, a 60,000-square-foot athletic and community center, featuring a regulation-size NBA basketball court, training facilities and multipurpose rooms for meetings and events.

The Obama Foundation, which is headquartered at the center, also runs leadership, education and community programs in the United States and around the world, including initiatives to train emerging leaders, support young people and encourage civic engagement.

Obama's original presidential records are instead stored at the National Archives in College Park, Maryland, rather than at the Chicago campus, which is not part of the federally operated presidential library system.

Critics have long questioned why the city granted control of valuable public parkland for a privately operated museum and foundation headquarters rather than a traditional presidential library, although the plans were approved by the Chicago City Council and the Chicago Plan Commission. The arrangement faced years of legal challenges that ultimately failed to stop construction, although opponents maintained that the courts never ruled on the merits of their central argument that the use of public parkland violated Illinois' public trust doctrine.
The foundation has promoted the center as far more than a museum, describing it as a place to develop future leaders and inspire change around the world.
"We are building more than a campus. We are creating a living institution that will inspire, empower, and connect the next generation of leaders," the foundation stated in its 2024 annual report.
Obama echoed that vision during the center's June opening ceremony , saying it was designed to be more than a monument to his presidency.
"We designed the center not to be some lifeless mausoleum," Obama said.
"While we are non-partisan, we are not value-neutral. We have a point of view."
